summary: RFC 5440 defines the Include Route Object in PCEP to specify network elements a computed path must traverse, but does not say whether its subobject list is ordered. This standards-track RFC clarifies that.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo clarifies that a PCEP Include Route Object lists nodes in order and that its L bit marks a loose hop. These rules help clients and path-computation elements interpret requested routes consistently.

questions: is the pcep include route object ordered
what does the l bit mean in an iro
subtitle: Clarifies the order of PCEP Include Route Object subobjects and meaning of the L bit.

tldr.problem: RFC 5440 did not specify whether an Include Route Object's subobjects were ordered or how its L bit should be interpreted.
tldr.mechanism: The update defines IRO contents as an ordered list and uses the L bit to distinguish loose from strict hops.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7896 updates RFC 5440 and explains interoperability problems that can occur with implementations using the earlier ambiguity.

today: RFC 7896 is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 5440. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 7896.

sections.title: Ambiguity in the Include Route Object
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) lets a Path Computation Client (PCC) communicate with a Path Computation Element (PCE), or lets two PCEs communicate. RFC 5440 defines an Include Route Object (IRO) to name network elements a computed path should traverse, but does not say whether the subobjects are ordered and says the L bit has no meaning within an IRO.

RFC 7896 updates the IRO specification to establish a standard representation for interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: A route request can list network nodes that a path should include. This memo clarifies the order of that list and the meaning of a flag on each item.

sections.title: Ordered Nodes and Loose or Strict Hops
sections.content: An IRO contains an ordered list of subobjects representing a series of abstract nodes. The L bit is set when a subobject represents a loose hop and is clear when it represents a strict hop. The meaning of loose and strict follows the referenced RSVP-TE specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Read the IRO items in the order they appear. A set L bit marks a loose hop; a clear bit marks a strict hop.

sections.title: Operational Interoperability
sections.content: Some implementations may always interpret IRO subobjects as loose because RFC 5440 was unclear. If a PCC assumes loose hops but a conforming PCE treats them as strict, the PCE may fail to find a path. If a conforming PCC requests strict hops from a non-conforming PCE, that PCE may return a path that violates the requested hops, and the PCC may use an incorrect path.
sections.plainLanguage: If the PCC and PCE disagree about whether a hop is strict, the path may fail or may not follow the requested route. The update defines a shared interpretation.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The update introduces no new security considerations beyond those in RFC 5440. It notes that clarifying ordering and loose-hop handling has no negative security impact, and that PCEP operates over TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says these clarifications add no security concerns beyond those already covered in RFC 5440.
